A1.justification: Both PDFs are complete 33-page versions of the same paper. Their text, equations, figures, tabular summaries and Appendices A–C support reliable comparison.

before.justification: v2 reports original neural-network experiments across five runs in Section 2.3/Figure 3 and numerical optimization comparisons in Figures 2 and 4.

after.justification: v3 retains the same original neural-network experiments and numerical optimization results, including Figure 4 in Appendix C.2.

M1.justification: The heavy-ball ODE, Nesterov updates, stochastic variants and AGNES scheme in Section 3 are identical.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same synthetic teacher–student regression data, two-dimensional optimization example and one-dimensional examples in Appendix C.2. No evaluated task or scenario changes.

E2.justification: Gradient descent remains the comparator to Nesterov’s algorithm in Appendix C.2/Figure 4. No evaluated comparator is added, removed or replaced.

E3.justification: The experimental settings are identical, including 100 points in 12 dimensions, network architectures, 10,000 training epochs, learning rate 0.005 and momentum 0.99 in Section 2.3. The numerical-example settings also match.

E4.justification: The step-size and limit-point illustration in Figure 2, loss-landscape analysis in Figure 3 and parameter sensitivity comparison in Figure 4 are unchanged.

E5.justification: Both report five runs and display separate random-initialization curves in Figure 3. Run information and uncertainty reporting are unchanged; neither adds confidence intervals or significance tests.

E6.justification: All numerical results and plotted curves match. Both report final training losses between 10^-12 and 10^-9 and the same Figure 4 finding that gradient descent can outperform Nesterov near the strong-aiming threshold.

T1.justification: All assumptions, definitions, theorems and proofs, including Appendices A–C, are identical. Although v3 newly acknowledges Quentin Merigot for a simpler proof requiring less regularity, Lemma 7 and its Appendix A proof were already present unchanged in v2.

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution statement and conclusion retain identical claims about acceleration under benign non-convexity in continuous time and deterministic and stochastic discrete-time settings.

C2.justification: The interpretations and limitations are unchanged, including the local applicability of the geometric assumptions, the imperfect gradient-direction proxy and the restrictive affine-projection assumption for discrete-time guarantees.

D1.justification: The architecture, training hyperparameters and finite-difference implementation details in Section 2.3 are identical. No code or data access information is added or removed.

R1.justification: The bibliography, related-work discussion and novelty positioning are identical. The new personal acknowledgement adds attribution without changing cited works or research positioning.

P1.justification: v3 adds a short Acknowledgements section before References, crediting NSF grant DMS 2424801 and Quentin Merigot, and updates the arXiv version/date stamp. The remaining prose and section organization are unchanged.

P2.justification: The acknowledgements shift the bibliography’s placement and page breaks across pages 11–13. All figures, tabular summaries, captions and appendix layouts remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: v3 adds funding and contributor acknowledgements with minor reference-layout changes. The credited proof already appears identically in v2, and all scientific content, empirical evidence, explanations and limitations remain unchanged. The attribution update does not meaningfully alter overall paper quality.
